## Overview

Steven Tan sent me some proposals for an AI Harness for developing clinical SAS code and generating outputs.  We have a meeting on August 14th at 8:30am to discuss it.  These are my notes to prepare for the discussion and notes about the meeting.

## Harness

- Harness is the controlled workspace for executing AI workflows
- Keeps human in the loop for judgement calls
- Harness includes approved inputs, standards, programs, SAS control, QC, evidence, etc.  Produces artifacts. 
- Harness submits a program to a SAS environment and captures the result

## Run flow - "the unit"

In double-programmed unit, two programs would build the same deliverable independently from the same specifications

1.  Work order - spec sheet
2.  Freeze and prepare - hash the inputs, standards, environmental prep
3.  Execute in SAS
4.  Check, validation
5.  Review and release

## Folder structure

1.  Inputs: raw/transfers/specs - frozen, read only
2.  Standards and Rules - He mixes RAG type references and rules/skills into this section.  Essentially this is the contents of the .claude directory.  Includes macros
3.  Unit Work orders
    - yaml based
4.  Programs
    - adae.sas, adsl.sas, etc.
5.  Outputs
    - xpt/sas7bdat
6.  Run evidence
    - Harness-specific logs, SAS logs, .lst files
7.  Findings and reruns
    - various reporting structures
8.  Human review
    - various review structures
9.  Release package


## Small-scale clinical programming pilot

A fixed price pilot for one specific clinical-programming workflow in the client's approved environment.

**Product**: 12 named programming units in one workflow, each delivered against agreed specifications, checks, and review steps.  The client chooses the unit type before the pilot begins.

Example Units:
    -  SDTM Domain Unit - one named mapped domain, metadata, agreed checks, and QC evidence
    -  ADaM Dataset
    -  TFL
    -  Conformance-check - set of checks against one frozen artifact with finding triage and document disposition


## The Wu Consulting Harness process flow

1.  Agreed SOW, deliverable and project specs, all these details
2.  **Harness**: where the magic happens
3.  Human work product:  ?Wu? programmer evaluates and reviews for delivery.

## Pricing:
    - $43k for a 12-unit pilot
    - $3.5k for each individual unit


### My thoughts

1.  Is this built yet?  What is the actual architecture of the system?  Where does the AI live?  This is important for HIPPA and pricing. Using Bedrock/Foundry, we pay for use and this can get expensive, especially if we are working iteratively on a "pilot".  Expenses decline after POC is completed.

2.  What is the UI/UX?  I am picturing some kind of full-stack web application with an attractive submission AI, real time progress updates, dashboard, etc.  Not a heavy lift to develop this from scratch, more of an issue for deployment that fits within their environment.

3.  AI Support structure: What is built and what needs to be built?  These are mostly fixed artifacts.  Client specific standards are added on top of these. We need the following:
    -  Knowledge base RAG
    -  Skills and rules
    -  development agents
    -  QC/review agents
    -  Project planning agents


4.  These client specific standards, spec sheets, policies.  We need some sort of ingestion pathway.  I would assume this would be built into the application, but they would need to be autoingested into a special project RAG.

5.  AI Harness:  This is the tricky one.  If we built this out in claude code, a lot of the work is done because Claude Code is the harness.  But this isn't really a marketable product, it is more of a service our clients could buy from us (i.e., programmer time, we just do it fast).  To make this a true harness, we need to build a lot of this from scratch.  Doable, but this is what is going to take the time because bare AI APIs are a little weird off the shelf..  However, it does allow us some model flexibility and the ability for multi-model systems.
    -  Adversarial Anthropic vs OpenAI can review each other using the same baseline data, compensating for whatever holes are each model
    -  Possibility of offering multi-model double programming.  More closely simulates a true human double programming.  If we submit the same context to a single model, we won't get exactly the same result, but we aren't really validating anything since the prompt uses the same model weights.

6.  Service vs product offering:
    -  The service side is the easiest, we monitor the progress at each step and make the thing work.
    -  Product side needs a lot of validation to make it work.  Typical budget is 30-60 days to build the system, and several months of fine tuning.  Requires the following:
        - System prompt: this is trickier than it sounds
        - Rules/Skills development - easy for a first pass, but require a lot of optimization

7.  How I would make this work:
    -  AWS Bedrock access to a multi-model endpoint.  HIPPA compliant, can be easily transferred to a client via an IAM role.
    -  Hosted application, owned by Wu consulting environment.  Client initialization will include a configuration file that grants access to client cloud endpoints.  Technically, all data stays inside client environment, only the UI/Server logic is external.
    -  Bonus points if the data ingestion pathway could include any completed SAS workflows from the client.  If they are working on a specific medication or domain, example code sets will go a long way to making this better.

8.  If the interface system is already built:
    -  we need to develop the actual algorithm, and I would model this after my claude CDISC workflow.  

    -  Agent structure
        -  orchestration/planning agent: translates the specs into an AI-friendly spec
        -  project plan reviewer agent: separate model that evaluates the original spec and AI-planning document, signs off or asks for revisions
        -  Data mapper agent:  Finds all the data required for transformations.  Ingests data and calculates distributions for all input variables.  These are read into a context structure for review.  This is important so the developer agents know what the data look like.
        -  stat programmer agent: follows the plan and data map to build each of the programs.  Follows a recursive algorithm: develop data chunk, runs, calculates results, compares to spec sheet, revises/repeats until meets the spec.  Move on to the next item.
        -  reporting agent: calculates crosstabs and statistics for each transformation, sorce->derivation and builds a reviewable document for a reviewer agent.
        -  Reviewer agent: code review, reviews output files for completeness, mostly structural reviews, not quality.
        -  Antagonistic reviewer:  This reviews for quality.  Ideally a different AI model.  Produces a report for human review, this is where human in the loop reviews the report and code and makes final decisions.
        -  Specialized agents:  TFLs, SAS Macros, PROC REPORT, CDISC expert, etc.
    
    - Skill structure:
        -  skill to review source data, what to produce
        -  spec sheet parsing - how to get the information ready for agents
        -  SAS skills - this is the tough one, because I don't think SAS is very AI friendly right now
        -  control skills: when to develop macros, when to stick to one-offs, style guides, directory and file structures, order of operations

    - Rule structure
        -  rules governing derivations:  always refer to source frequencies, then spec sheet for outcomes, recursive development to make them work
        -  rules governing evaluations - what is the acceptance criteria and what to do if it isn't met
        -  Rules governing data privacy, blinding, HIPPA compliance, etc.
